name: F-4 Phantom II
tagline: 5,195 built - the West's definitive Cold War fighter. Originally a gun-less US Navy fleet interceptor, it proved so capable that the US Air Force adopted it too, and it went on to fly fighter, bomber and reconnaissance missions for 11 nations, including the RAF and Royal Navy.
history: First flown on 27 May 1958, the Phantom set 16 world records - including a 1,606 mph absolute speed record and a zoom climb to over 98,000 ft ('Operation Top Flight') - before dominating US procurement in the 1960s. In Vietnam it was the principal US air-superiority and strike aircraft, and hard lessons about missile reliability and the lack of an internal gun (fixed in the F-4E) reshaped Western fighter design and created Top Gun and Red Flag. Britain operated Rolls-Royce Spey-engined Phantoms from 1968 to 1992, including for Falklands-era air defence of the islands from 1982. The USAF retired its last QF-4 target drones in 2016, while Greece, Türkiye and Iran still fly small upgraded fleets today.
quickFacts: With 5,195 built, the Phantom is the most-produced American supersonic aircraft in history.
Its unflattering nicknames - 'Rhino', 'Double Ugly', 'the flying brick' - came with an affectionate saying: it was proof that with enough thrust, even a brick can fly.
Both the USAF Thunderbirds and US Navy Blue Angels flew the Phantom simultaneously in 1969-1973, the only type ever shared by both teams.
The UK's Phantoms were unique: re-engined with Rolls-Royce Spey turbofans, which made them shorter-legged at altitude but gave brutal low-level thrust.
Phantom crews scored 277+ air-to-air kills in Vietnam alone; the only US aces of the war - one Navy crew and three USAF airmen - all flew F-4s.
The last US Phantoms died as QF-4 target drones, with the final unmanned shoot-down flight in 2016 - 58 years after first flight.

overview: The McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II is an American twin-engine, two-seat fighter-bomber built by McDonnell Douglas. It was originally armed with no internal gun, and more than 5,000 were built - more than any other Western supersonic fighter.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

It served the US Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps simultaneously, set 16 world records, and fought from Vietnam to the Iran-Iraq War. In 2026, 68 years after its first flight, it remains in combat-alert service with three air forces.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

sections.heading: Origins & Concept
paragraphs: The Phantom began as a company gamble: McDonnell, with no Navy fighter contract after the F3H, designed a big twin-engined all-weather attack aircraft on its own initiative in 1953 and kept reshaping it to whatever the Navy hinted it might want. What the Navy finally wanted, in 1955, was a fleet-defence interceptor: two seats, powerful radar, and missiles - no gun - to kill bombers far from the carrier.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

The result flew in May 1958 and promptly demolished expectations: the XF4H-1 beat Vought's single-seat Crusader III in the fly-off partly because its second crewman tamed the radar workload, and the production F4H began setting world records almost as a hobby - absolute altitude (98,557 ft, Operation Top Flight), absolute speed (1,606 mph, Operation Skyburner), and low-altitude speed records that stood for decades.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

sections.heading: Development
paragraphs: The record-smashing embarrassed the Air Force into an unprecedented step: adopting a Navy fighter. Defence Secretary McNamara's push for tri-service commonality made the F-4C the USAF's new standard, and the Phantom became the rare aircraft flown by the Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps at once.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

Vietnam rewrote the design. Missile-only armament proved a doctrinal fantasy against agile MiGs at knife range, so the definitive USAF F-4E of 1967 added an internal 20mm cannon and slatted wings for manoeuvring. Reconnaissance RF-4s, Wild Weasel F-4Gs that hunted missile radars, and export variants for eleven nations rounded out a 5,195-aircraft run - production ending in 1981 in St. Louis and 1981 in Japan under licence.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

sections.heading: Combat History
paragraphs: Vietnam made the Phantom's legend and exposed its flaws in equal measure. It flew everything - MiG sweeps, bombing, close support, reconnaissance, Weasel work - and claimed the great majority of American air-to-air kills, including all five American aces of the war among its crews. The frustrations (missiles that failed, the missing gun, smoke trails visible for miles) drove reforms like Top Gun{{ref:wiki-topgun}} that reshaped Western air combat training.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

Israeli Phantoms carried the brunt of the War of Attrition and the 1973 Yom Kippur War's desperate strike missions; Iranian F-4s - delivered to the Shah - flew hard through the entire Iran-Iraq War and remain in Iranian service today. USAF Phantoms soldiered through Desert Storm as Wild Weasels, retiring from American combat service in 1996.{{ref:wiki-f4}}
Sixty-eight years after its first flight, Phantoms still stand alert in Türkiye, Greece and Iran, upgraded with modern radars and weapons.{{ref:tw-phantom}}

sections.heading: Design & Engineering
paragraphs: Nothing about the Phantom is subtle. Two J79 turbojets delivered 35,700 lb of combined afterburning thrust; the wings gained their signature 12-degree upturned tips and the tailplane its 23-degree droop as pragmatic fixes for stability problems found in the wind tunnel - giving the aircraft its unmistakable bent silhouette.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

It hauled fighter-sized speed with bomber-sized loads: over 18,000 lb of ordnance on nine hardpoints, more than a WWII B-17 carried. The second seat, mocked at first, proved the aircraft's quiet advantage - two brains dividing radar, weapons and lookout duties in an era when automation offered no help.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

sections.heading: Legacy
paragraphs: The Phantom taught the West most of what it knows about modern air combat, largely by getting there first and making the instructive mistakes: missiles need guns behind them, training beats technology, and a great fighter is a great sensor-and-weapons truck. Its successors - F-14, F-15, F/A-18 - are all, in different ways, answers to questions the F-4 posed.{{ref:wiki-f4}}

With over 5,000 built and service on every continent except Antarctica, the Phantom became shorthand for Western air power itself for a generation - and its nickname among former crews, 'Phantom Phorever', persists in veteran circles. Three air forces still fly it today.{{ref:tw-phantom}}{{ref:nasm-f4}}

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Operation Bolo MiG trap
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: USAF F-4C Phantoms disguised their flight profile and callsigns to mimic a vulnerable strike package, luring North Vietnamese MiG-21s into a fight in which seven MiG-21s were shot down in about 12 minutes with no U.S. losses.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Duarte mid-air collision with Hughes Airwest Flight 706
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: A US Marine Corps F-4B flying under visual rules with an inoperative transponder collided with a climbing DC-9 airliner over the San Gabriel Mountains. All 49 people on the airliner and the Phantom's pilot were killed; only the radar intercept officer ejected in time.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Israeli friendly-fire shootdown
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: During the Yom Kippur War, an Israeli Nesher pilot mistakenly identified a retreating Israeli F-4 as a hostile MiG-21 and shot it down. The crew ejected and were rescued from the Mediterranean.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Crash into a Yokohama neighbourhood
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: A U.S. Marine Corps RF-4B suffered an in-flight engine fire and crashed into a residential neighbourhood in Yokohama, Japan. Both crew ejected safely, but two children in the house were killed and their mother later died of crash-related injuries.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: RAF Phantom shoots down an RAF Jaguar
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: A 92 Squadron Phantom accidentally launched a Sidewinder at a Jaguar over West Germany during an exercise intercept. The Jaguar pilot ejected safely; the Phantom crew were court-martialled.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Shootdown by Syrian air defences
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: A Turkish Air Force RF-4E reconnaissance Phantom was shot down by Syrian air defences over the Mediterranean Sea after briefly entering Syrian airspace during a radar-testing mission. Both crew were killed.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Tanagra airshow display crash
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: A Hellenic Air Force F-4E Phantom II of 338 Squadron, 117th Combat Wing, crashed during its aerobatic display at the Athens Flying Week airshow at Tanagra Air Base, coming down in open ground a few kilometres from the base after appearing to lose altitude coming out of a low-level turn. The crew did not eject and both were killed; no spectators or ground personnel were hurt. The Hellenic Air Force grounded the display and said the cause was under investigation, and Greece observed three days of national mourning.
